publications.title: Energy To Grow: Securing New Zealand's Future
publications.description:
Aotearoa New Zealand’s energy system remains one of the best in the world, but it is now at a crossroads. Over the past 50 years, New Zealand’s affordable, secure energy supply has powered industrial growth and sustained economic competitiveness. But that advantage is now under pressure.

This report sets out how New Zealand can renew its competitive edge with abundant, firmed renewable energy – powering economic growth while navigating the challenges of affordability, security and sustainability.

publications.title: Growing Our Advantage in Agritech

publications.title: For US Insurers, Tariffs Create Risks and Opportunities
publications.description:
Sharing BCG’s latest piece, For US Insurers, Tariffs Create Risks and Opportunities, which outlines how evolving trade policy is reshaping the insurance landscape. The US trade tariffs affect everything from claims underwriting to investment returns. But there's an opportunity for companies that navigate the changes successfully. 

Key takeaways: 
• As imports of steel, electronics and other goods become pricier, the cost of resolving P&C claims rises—particularly for auto and home repairs. 
• Market volatility could affect the insurers' investment portfolios, particularly companies with long-tail commercial lines. 
• P&C insurers must adapt their scenario planning to become more resilient as trade policies change. 
 
The article offers a clear breakdown of what’s at stake—and how insurers can prepare. Worth a read for anyone tracking market risk.

headline: BCG, COP28 Action Agenda on Regenerative Landscapes
about:
I'm a Partner & Associate Director in Sustainable Food & Agriculture at BCG. I joined our company in 2013 and have worked in the New York, Copenhagen, Chicago, and London offices.

On a day-to-day basis, I oversee the Action Agenda on Regenerative Landscapes (AARL) on behalf of BCG. Launched at COP28, AARL is a new paradigm of collaboration that brings together over 30 of the world’s leading food and agriculture organizations to break down barriers to a more sustainable and resilient food system through landscape-level action. The initiative is co-chaired by COP28, UN High Level Champions, World Business Council on Sustainable Development, and Boston Consulting Group. 

To date, AARL has brought together leading organizations that are activating 300+ landscape projects across 210m hectares and 110 countries, with $9B in committed investment by 2030. In 2025, AARL launched the Landscape Accelerator Brazil (LAB) to accelerate the regenerative transformation of key Brazilian landscapes – starting in the Cerrado and the Amazon – to ubild generational benefits for producers, net‑positive outcomes for climate and nature, and more resilient supply chains. 

In addition to this role, I work with consumer packaged companies and agrifood organizations on their sustainable operations. I am passionate about food systems transformation and have supported clients in developing strategies to harness sustainability for competitive advantage, including reimagining business models for sustainability and circularity, scaling regenerative agriculture, decarbonizing supply chains, and operationalizing sustainable packaging.

publications.title: Dedicated hardware accelerators for the epistatic analysis of human genetic data
publications.description: The recent advances in genomic microarrays design provide the possibility to retrieve hundreds of thousands of significative genetic features from patients at affordable costs. Understanding if non-linear interactions (epistatic relationships) between these features determine or not the arising of complex common multifactorial genetic diseases is a critical task for human geneticists. The algorithms able to detect such relationships, like the Multifactor Dimensionality Reduction (MDR) algorithm, are computationally expensive and their practical utility is very often limited by the amount of time required by the analysis. This paper presents three hardware-accelerated implementations of the MDR algorithm, tailored for many-core processors, Xilinx Virtex-5 FPGAs and generic GPUs respectively. These implementations provide timing performance improvements of up to two magnitude orders with respect to the software implementation.

publications.title: Distributed Energy - A Disruptive Force
publications.description: Distributed Energy (DE) is becoming a disruptive force in the U.S. power business. So far, DE's growth has relied on subsidies, lower costs and improvements in technology. As the industry matures, much of its future growth will be driven by business model innovations, such as leasing models, financing tools that lowers cost of capital and improved targeting and segmentation of customers. Utilities' primacy in the generation and delivery of electricity is under attack. To stay competitive, utilities must proactively respond to a future with more DE. Utilities have multiple advantages they can mobilize, but they must do so quickly.

publications.title: Driving Efficiency in Retail Energy Sales: Simplify, Streamline, Focus
publications.description:
For retail energy companies, maximizing the efficiency of sales efforts, including customer service, can be essential to winning in today’s highly competitive, price-sensitive environment. Many organizations struggle with the challenge, however. This holds particularly true for the industry’s bigger companies. A recent benchmarking by The Boston Consulting Group (BCG) revealed that large retail-energy businesses often spend materially more than smaller companies to win and keep customers. Large companies also often fail to capture the scale-related advantages that their size should afford, forfeiting what could be a significant source of competitive advantage.
What are the keys to achieving best-in-class execution in retail energy sales—for large energy companies and smaller ones alike? Our study, which examined more than 30 companies across Australia, Europe, and the U.S., found commonalities among top practitioners. (See “Benchmarking Details.”) On a high level, companies with the most advantageous cost structures typically possess several key attributes: a simplified business model, a relatively narrow focus in terms of customer targeting and product offerings, streamlined business processes, a commitment to customer-service excellence, delayered organizations, and a leadership-driven culture that places a high value on simplification. These companies have, in essence, chosen to do less but do better—and are seeing measurable results in their top and bottom lines as a result.

publications.title: Achieving Excellence in Energy Networks
publications.description:
Around the world there is a growing focus on energy networks and operators’ responsibility for the planning, construction, and maintenance of grids and pipelines. Achieving operational excellence has become an imperative as a result of increasing investment as well as regulatory and customer pressures—all occurring in an economically constrained environment. Utilities are challenged to go beyond achieving savings on narrow functions to develop a holistic approach that achieves true excellence—both cost efficiency and quality improvement.

Investment dynamics are exerting new pressures on operators. In developed countries, key drivers include the replacement of aging infrastructure (much of which is more than 50 years old and increasingly subject to failure), the interconnection of regions and states, and the reinforcement necessary for the integration of renewable-power generation. In developing countries, the key driver is grid expansion to cope with the expected increase in per capita electricity consumption as a result of accelerating urbanization and industrialization.

In addition, the rise of smart-grid development has important ramifications for energy networks worldwide. NRG Expert estimates that global capital expenditures in power transmission and distribution will grow 5 percent anually in the coming years, reaching more than $220 billion by 2015.

Regulators continue to put pressure on network operators to reduce costs. Thus, it has become standard practice to incorporate efficiency factors in the regulation of energy networks. For example, over the past 15 years, most European countries have moved from cost-plus to performance-based regulation, which allows network operators to keep the profits made through reductions in operating costs—as long as they achieve or exceed the efficiency target. Achieving savings is becoming particularly hard in some countries where such regimes are well established and the low-hanging fruit has already been picked.

publications.title: Mind the Gap: What Scenario Analysis Says About the Future of the U.S. Power Industry
publications.description:
The U.S. electric-power market is inching closer to a major shortfall in generating capacity. This is troublesome in itself but what is causing perhaps even more concern for both the industry and the country’s broader economy is the magnitude of uncertainty related to alternative ways to address the supply gap. This uncertainty may translate into taking too few or insufficiently concrete steps, and thus it has serious implications for the reliability of the nation’s power grid.

Although the U.S. economy was recently hit by a recession, the demand for electric power continues to grow. And the story is also complicated on the supply side: how will recent and future changes in technology and emissions regulations impact the competitive mix in electric-power generation sources?

A number of new and existing variables are clouding the future of the U.S. electric-power industry primarily by exacerbating the uncertainty about policy and the prices power companies will require to justify making big investments in new generation capacity. The advent of new technology and drilling methods has made the U.S. the world’s leading producer of natural gas, allowing gas to approach coal’s share of the country’s power-generation fuel mix. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, the states, and the courts continue to battle fiercely over rules for curbing power plant emissions of carbon dioxide, mercury, and other pollutants. The nuclear industry has been in a state of anxiety since Japan’s Fukushima nuclear accident in March 2011. And the renewable-energy business is feeling insecure as a result of waning federal-government support and crumbling power prices due to falling natural-gas prices.

publications.title: Capturing the Value of Smart Meters
publications.description:
Smart meters hold considerable promise for utilities. They can drive down costs, increase transparency for customers, and enable flexible pricing. But they are destined to disappoint unless utilities can solve a fundamental challenge: engaging the customer. Much of the business case for smart meters hinges on convincing customers to genuinely change their energy usage—and this is far easier said than done. Utilities will need to mount a comprehensive communication and change-management campaign if they hope to get the necessary buy-in.

Informed by proprietary consumer research, this essay looks at the current environment for smart-meter deployment and the specific imperative to gain customer buy-in.

publications.title: Utility M&A: Beating the Odds
publications.description:
Merger and acquisition (M&A) activity in the U.S. electric-utility industry has increased over the past year and a half following the 2005 repeal of the Public Utility Holding Company Act (PUHCA). Several high-profile deals have been announced; some have been successful, and others, such as the Constellation–FPL Group and Exelon–PSEG (Public Service Enterprise Group) deals, became ensnared in the state regulatory process. The primary question is not whether M&A will continue but whether utility executives are prepared to manage increasingly complex regulatory challenges.

The reality is that M&A activity is (and always has been) one of several tools available to utility CEOs to reshape their portfolios and meet their shareholders’ expectations for returns. Other equally important tools include operational improvement programs, investment in growth of the rate base, reshaping the rate structure, and pursuing focused, unregulated organic growth. Among those alternatives, M&A is the most potent, publicly visible, and often irreversible option that a CEO can deploy. However, M&A has too often been applied reflexively—much like the hammer that sees everything as a nail.

publications.title: Economic Assessment of Used Nuclear Fuel Management in the United States
publications.description:
Governments and industry have debated several options for managing used fuel in the 40 years during which nuclear power generation has spread across the industrial world. Countries using nuclear energy have adopted different strategies ― some pursuing a “recycling” strategy in which used nuclear fuel is treated and then reused as a component of new reactor fuel and some pursuing a “once-through” strategy in which untreated used fuel is stored, later to be emplaced in a permanent geological repository.

For the last 20 years, the U.S. have pursued development of a geologic repository for used fuel disposal ― the once-through strategy ― at Yucca Mountain in Nevada. The key benefits of that strategy are: a) capacity to handle all legacy used fuel (estimated at 54,000 metric tons in 2005, currently stored at nuclear power plants); b) capacity to handle additional used fuel discharged after a period of cooling and interim storage, provided that additional repository capacity is available; and c) no further need for handling or processing of used fuel after disposal which, to that extent, makes the once-through strategy a complete lifecycle solution.

DOE 2001 cost estimates for a U.S. repository that is capable of storing a total quantity of 83,800 tons of commercial used fuel indicate a lifecycle investment of about $46B[--DOE undiscounted life cycle cost estimates are reported to 2005 $ and netted of estimated cost to dispose of non-commercial
 nuclear waste.--], not including costs for interim storage at power plants. Over the last decade, however, several factors have led to questions about the appropriateness of the once-through fuel cycle as an exclusive used fuel management strategy.

publications.title: Preparing for Fundamental Shifts in Energy: Strategies for a Changing Industry
publications.description:
New trends in economics, geopolitics, industry behavior, and technology are causing fundamental shifts in the energy landscape. For industry players, these shifts pose a significant threat and opportunity at the same time. Some players will be able to take advantage of these shifts, but many others will destroy value for investors and other stakeholders.

These new competitive forces are changing the balance of power between sellers and buyers and destabilizing established businesses.  Succeeding in this volatile environment demands fresh insight and creativity, as well as new capabilities and new business skills. But change can be risky when the stakes are high.

Despite the risk, energy companies must continue to place their bets, making enormous long-term investments and necessary short-term commitments.

publications.title: Attack and Defense: Managing the Competitive Cycle in Telecom
publications.description:
The unprecedented bull market in technology, media, and telecommunications stocks has given way in recent months to a dramatic weakening in valuations. The speed of this decline took most industry executives by surprise. Early in 2000, capital was cheap and plentiful for new entrants who could claim boundless opportunity. Since then, however, private equity has largely dried up. At the same time, established players have been forced to launch restructuring plans in response to weakened credit ratings, which in some cases were triggered by the soaring costs associated with next-generation mobile licenses.

Although much has changed in recent months, some things remain the same. In particular, two core trends in customer demand continue unabated: the spread of Internet protocol-based services (IP) and the expansion of mobile communications. Together they are transforming the telecommunications industry. As consumer demand for IP and mobile services explodes, virtually every business process from product development to sales and marketing to provisioning will require reworking. In addition, much of the existing network capacity will become redundant as more efficient technologies are adopted.

As the technology, media, and telecom industries evolve, which companies will emerge as winners? Until recently, there were two opposing sets of market participants, each with its own philosophy.

headline: Managing Director & Senior Partner at Boston Consulting Group (BCG)
about:
Perry Keenan is a member of the global leadership team for the People & Organization practice area at Boston Consulting Group. 

Perry commenced his BCG career as an Associate in the Auckland office in 1988. He then spent extensive time working across the BCG Asia system during the 1990s. He returned to BCG New Zealand in 1999, leading it for six years before transferring to BCG Chicago. He then played a crucial role in developing BCG’s Change Management Topic, which he went on to lead globally for more than a decade.

From 2011 through 2017, Perry was also a BCG Fellow researching the factors that materially and systematically improve change management odds—and, in fact, flip them dramatically in favor of success. 

Perry is a featured expert for Brightline, a Project Management Institute (PMI) initiative dedicated to helping executives bridge the expensive and unproductive gap between strategy design and delivery.

Perry has coauthored several influential articles with the Project Management Institute and Harvard Business Review, including "Strategic Initiative Management – The PMO Imperative" and “The Hard Side of Change Management”; one of HBR’s most read articles on Change Management, additionally he is a contributing author to HBR's "Ten Must Reads On Change Management" series.
 	
For this work and his ongoing contributions to the field of engineering, Perry has been recognized as a Fellow of the Institution of Mechanical Engineers (UK), a Fellow of the Institution of Engineering and Technology (UK) and a Fellow of Engineering New Zealand.

publications.title: How GenAI Reimagines Supply Chain Management
publications.description: Generative AI lets companies capture previously untapped benefits of AI in supply chains. By simplifying user interfaces, automating operations and decision making, and generating actionable insights from large data sets, GenAI overcomes the complexities of earlier AI implementations and promotes higher adoption

publications.title: Rapidly Unlock Value with Warehouse Excellence
publications.description: Digital platforms dominate the modern marketplace, but commerce still hinges on the physical exchange of goods, with warehousing playing a critical role as the last interface with the customer. Excellence in warehousing can unlock substantial value and provide a competitive edge through efficient operations, digitization, and automation. BCG’s integrated approach delivers significant service improvements while cutting costs without capital investments.

publications.title: Lessons from Baltimore for Supply Chain Resilience
publications.description: Right now, the collapse of the Francis Scott Key Bridge in Baltimore, which has largely closed one of the biggest ports on the eastern seaboard of the US, is underlining the importance of supply chain resilience. Resilience was a priority for CEOs during the height and immediate aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic. And recent events have now brought the need for adaptable supply chains sharply back into focus.

publications.title: Breaking the Reactionary Cycle by Investing in Supply Chain Resilience
publications.publishedAt: Journal of Supply Chain Management, Logistics & Procurement · Jun 24, 2023
publications.description: Supply chain resilience has long been valued, yet often deprioritized in favor of cost reduction during stable times. Short-term fixes like inventory buildup have been the go-to response to disruptions, while structural changes such as nearshoring or capacity expansion were avoided due to unclear ROI. However, with climate change and geopolitical instability making disruptions the ‘new normal,’ supply chain leaders must balance resilience with cost, capital, and service-level goals. This paper examines resilience capabilities based on a benchmarking study by BCG and APQC, offering guidance for developing strategies tailored to individual risk profiles.

publications.title: Customers’ Willingness to Pay Can Turn the Tide Toward Decarbonized Shipping
publications.description: BCG surveyed 125 companies that ship cargo to gauge their willingness to pay a premium for carbon-neutral shipping. Their responses present both challenges and opportunities for the shipping industry.

publications.title: Emphasize Resilience in Supply Chains
publications.description: Today’s conditions bring more complexity to the operations officer role—perhaps even redefining it—as businesses face the threat of economic slowdown while trying to find new opportunities. Here’s why and how supply chain leaders who strive for visibility, rapid response, and resilience can guide a company through these trying conditions.

publications.title: Riding the Rails to Sustainability
publications.description: Rail is the most sustainable mode of transport. Increasing its share of passengers and freight is critical to achieving net-zero goals.

publications.title: How to fix broken supply chains
publications.description: In the face of disruptions, how do we make sure supply chains can keep up? In this TED talk, I share a combination of solutions—from companies sharing risk to better forecasting disruptions—to help create a more resilient, efficient tomorrow.

publications.title: Global Shipping’s Net-Zero Transformation Challenge
publications.description: As you craft a decarbonization strategy—for today and tomorrow—here are seven crucial areas to consider.

publications.title: How Does PSR Affect Railroads’ Response to COVID-19?
publications.description: Railroads are fortunate to have upped their operational game with PSR given the drop in demand associated with COVID-19.  The landscape will change continuously, so the operating rhythm will need to get even faster for time being.  Planning now to compete for all-too-scarce freight during the recovery, and anticipating potential sudden shifts in demand are essential.  And codifying what was learned - and what they would do differently next time - is an opportunity that railroads should not pass up.

publications.title: Taking the Railroad Playbook Beyond PSR
publications.description: PSR has helped to fuel unprecedented financial returns, and better operating performance, for North American freight railroads.  But investors expect sustained improvements, and shippers will increasingly expect new capabilities.  The next wave of improvement will need to build on the efficiency gains of the past with a greater focus on commercial excellence and digital capabilities, and balance the focus on growth and efficiency.

publications.title: Preparing for North America’s New Auto Trade Rules
publications.description: We can model and anticipate what a post-NAFTA world will look like for automotive industry players.  But the answer depends on each company's supply chain configuration.  The key is to know possible outcomes - and shape them if possible - to turn what is a risk into potential advantage.

publications.title: Shifting Trade Rules and the Future of North America’s Auto Industry
publications.description: A change to NAFTA is a change, first and foremost, to the automotive industry.  Margins are thin and capital investments are long-lived.  Tariffs and transportation have the potential to turn a home-run of an investment into a corporate burden.

publications.title: Winners and Losers in a Post-NAFTA World
publications.description: While trade and tariff changes are mostly viewed as a negative shock to US manufacturers, they can also upset the hierarchy of competitive advantage within an industry.  It's important to know where you stand now, and where you might end up, relative to your competitors when it comes to your cost position so that you can prepare accordingly and make proactive and preemptive - not just reactive - moves.

publications.title: Three Things CEOs Should Do Now to Prepare for the New NAFTA
publications.description: This is not going to "blow over".  The Trump administration and other stakeholders are pushing for a change in the trade regime.  CEOs need to become Chief Supply Chain Officers and corporate diplomats for a while and ensure that they know how their supply chains could be impacted, try to shape what's happening, and ensure that their teams have a playbook to run depending on the outcome.

publications.title: How to Thrive in an Era of Shifting Trade Policy
publications.description: Trade policy is going to be more turbulent, as the "liberal consensus", at least in the US, seems to have weakened.  But companies can turn this to their advantage if they do their homework, and undertake some corporate diplomacy to ensure their voices are heard.

publications.title: A widened gaze at the Panama Canal
An Expanded Panama Canal Takes Logistics into Uncharted Waters

headline: Managing Director and Senior Partner at Boston Consulting Group (BCG) | Global BCG lead for Biopharma;  US lead for Public Sector Healthcare
about:
I am a core member of the Health Care and Public Sector practices at Boston Consulting Group. I have been at BCG for 21 years and in that time have worked extensively across all sectors of the health care industry. I am a member of the Health Care and Public Sector leadership teams and lead the firm’s Biopharma practice and US Public Sector Health Practice.

I am passionate about health care product and system innovation, access and affordability, and driving change. My work across the public and private sector is focused on these themes.

My biopharma work at BCG has spanned a range of topics across major biopharma companies, including corporate strategy, M&A, discovery and development innovation and productivity, medical affairs and regulatory. I have also partnered across the health care ecosystem on topics of value-based care, market access, affordability, and innovative models for access. I have worked across a full range of primary care and specialty TAs as well as a range of modalities including small molecules, vaccines, biologics and CGTs.

In the public sector, I have worked across various HHS agencies including CMS, FDA, NIH. I have led programs on topics including COVID response, vaccines and therapeutics, healthcare quality, pandemic preparedness and response, organizational effectiveness and change, data, and analytics.

Prior to joining BCG, I was a researcher and project analyst at Ligand Pharmaceuticals in San Diego.

headline: Consultant at BCG | Digital Strategy & Transformation | Chicago Booth MBA
about:
I am a Consultant at BCG, focused on business strategy and AI-driven problem solving.

At BCG, I work on technology-enabled transformation across industries, helping organizations apply AI and advanced analytics to improve productivity and decision-making. My work involves tackling ambiguous problems, identifying where AI can create real value, and shaping approaches that move beyond point solutions and can be adopted by teams in practice.

Prior to consulting, I was Managing Director of Product and Strategy at Easy Group, Canada’s largest tutoring company, where I led and grew cross-functional teams across product, platform, and operations while owning key transformation initiatives. I was deeply involved in building products and platforms from zero to one. Leading a rapidly growing team in a fast-moving industry grounded my perspective on execution, scalability, and translating strategy into day-to-day action.

I hold an MBA from Chicago Booth, with a background in economics and statistics. I am highly data-driven and particularly motivated by understanding how technology changes the way organizations and people work.

Prior to rejoining BCG, I was the president and CEO of Zappallas and COO of Oricon, both major digital service/entertainment companies in Japan. Over the course of my career, I have continued to be engaged in new business development, and have led launches of numerous new businesses leveraging digital technology.

I currently lead BCG Digital Ventures (BCG DV) in Asia Pacific. I also lead the Tokyo Center of BCG DV, which I led its establishment in April, 2016. Since then, I have been involved in generating new business ideas and new business building including capital investment. I also serve as an outside director for companies which BCG DV invested in.

I am a core member of BCG’s Technology, Media & Telecommunications and Consumer practices, and have worked closely mainly with clients in consumer and telecommunications industries. My project experiences include alliance support, growth strategy formulation and implementation support, and new business building especially in digital areas.

I've also worked at Walt Disney International Japan and at Mitsubishi Corporation, mainly doing business development, including launching of Cable & Satellite channel in Japan and Operating Leasing company in South America, the very first of its kind in the nation.

headline: Managing Director & Partner, BCG X | Data + Digital Platform, Digital Business Transformation, Team Building
about:
I am a Managing Director & Partner in Chicago, IL.  With 30+ years of experience, I bring a passion for helping organizations unlock business value and achieve step-function improvements in productivity, flexibility, and speed through technology.  
 
I have deep expertise managing large-scale digital transformations and delivering enterprise solutions across industries, such as Financial Services, Insurance, Consumer Packaged Goods, Retail, Health care and Defense.  Highlights of recent case work include the design, build, and implementation of a new core banking platform for a top direct bank, the architecture and development of a “digital front door” for a healthcare system, and ERP and PLM strategy and architecture for a large defense-related shipbuilder. 
 
As the global lead for BCG X Large Product & Platform Build moonshot, I am committed to building our delivery work while delivering outsized impact and value to our clients.
 
I initially joined BCG’s Chicago office in 2005, leaving in 2011 to lead the digital transformation of the consumer banking business at Discover and returning to BCG in 2016.   My prior experience also includes 11 years at Accenture, where I focused on ERP strategy and implementation and led the Software Intelligence team and Worldwide Center for Finance & Performance Management. 
 
I invite you to learn more about BCG X and our Digital and Technology work on LinkedIn, as well as by visiting BCG.com.

about:
Board Director, Fortune 500 Chief Risk Officer, Divisional CEO, General Manager, and Marketing EVP with a successful track record driving growth and building strong teams. Unique ability to bring a CEO’s perspective to risk management to enable speed, innovation, and resilience.  Deep knowledge of consumer finance, payments, risk, data, identity, fraud, and financial crimes services. 

Currently serves on the Board of Affirm (Nasdaq: AFRM) and is a member of the Audit and
Compensation Committees. Also a Senior Advisor to the Boston Consulting Group working with global banks, payments and technology/data companies to strengthen risk and drive growth. Advisor to a portfolio of growth-stage companies that are transforming risk management and identity/fraud services using AI, technology, and data. 

Previously served as Discover’s Chief Risk Officer, at the request of the CEO and Board, to drive a major transformation across Risk and Compliance.  Led several growth and turnaround businesses as a general manager / marketer, including SVP of Cardmember Marketing for Discover's $70B credit card business, General Manager of Discover’s $30B digital bank and deposits business, and CEO of HSBC's credit card business which spanned prime, sub-prime, co-brand, and private label.  Started with 10 years in strategy consulting, primarily with Booz-Allen & Hamilton.

Previously served on the Board Executive Committee of the Risk Management Association (now ProSight), an organization that provides education and networking to advance risk management practices.  Previously served on the Consumer Advisory Board of the CFPB to advise on regulatory policy.

Received an MBA with high honors from the Booth School of Business at The University of Chicago and a BS in Electrical Engineering with high honors from the University of Illinois.  Recently attended Stanford Law School's Directors College.

receivedRecommendations.description:
It is a privilege to recommend my friend, colleague, and mentor, Mr. Jon Kaplan. I worked with Jon for nearly 3 years at the Boston Consulting Group in Chicago; I know him well both as a friend and as a professional. He is the consummate professional and leads with three striking qualities: (1) extraordinary depth and breadth of experience, (2) unparalleled skills a listener, and (3) impressive clarity of thought.

First, Jon has been providing strategic advisory to leading firms around the globe for nearly his entire professional career. He has worked for numerous consultancies with hundreds of clients, and the results are the same: happy clients and impressive economic results. His experience stretches across all aspects of healthcare, and he has practical insights that drive results for clients. Very simply: I am often skeptical of the value of management consulting services. I am never skeptical of the value of Jon’s insight and value as an adviser.

Second, Jon is the best listener I know. Imagine you are working with Jon: his skill is not simply finishing your sentences or sitting quietly while you talk. He actively listens and facilitates you communicating with him. Jon makes it easy for you to explain complex, often subtle problems. His clients and teams notice this skill; it makes everyone around him better. I work every day to develop this listening skill Jon has demonstrated.

Third, Jon thinks and communicates with clarity. He listens well, and then he is able to summarize and simplify with precision and structure. Meetings with Jon never end without absolute clarity on the problem, the solution, and the approach.

It is this experience, listening skill, and ability to communicate with clarity that makes Jon the consultant’s consultant. He is the ultimate professional as well as a friend, mentor, and adviser, and I would recommend him without reservation. For questions, feel free to reach out to me directly at griffinrmyers@gmail.com.

The Workplace Wellness Alliance: Investing in a Sustainable Workforce
publications.description:
Employers—and developed economies—face three challenges to productivity: a talent shortage, an aging population, and the high incidence of chronic diseases.

Employers are uniquely positioned to improve health through the workplace, and workplace wellness initiatives can help address the challenges to productivity.

Workplace wellness initiatives help keep workers healthier longer, breaking the link between chronic diseases and aging while playing an important role in attracting and retaining talent

publications.title: The Workplace Wellness Alliance -- Collaborating to Improve Employees’ Health and Productivity
publications.description:
The economic cost of chronic disease, in terms of lost productivity, runs into the trillions of dollars each year.

Still, owing to the lack of information about the impact of specific tactics, companies have had a hard time justifying investments to improve employee wellness.

The Workplace Wellness Alliance, by providing a platform for collaboration, makes it easier for companies to home in on proven interventions.

publications.title: Reforming America’s Ailing Health-Care System  -- Market Lessons from a Social-Welfare System
publications.description:
The U.S. plan for health care reform focuses on the access, cost, and quality of care. 

To advance the quality of care, the United States could consider a “value-based” approach championed by Sweden. 

Sweden has created 69 extensive “disease registries” that enable medical professionals to evaluate care from multiple vantage points. 

The goal is to provide patients, doctors, and researchers a complete look at what works and what the costs are

about:
I am the founding global co-lead for BCG U, a new practice that focuses on helping our clients achieve high impact through accelerated capability development at scale for public and private organizations, as well as citizens at large. Our work involves developing highly sought-after digital skills that address fundamental mismatch in talent demand & supply at the enterprise and national levels, as well as critical capabilities necessary to fully unlock the benefits of large transformation programs.

Before joining BCG, I held various roles, including serving as the SEA system lead of BCG GAMMA (now BCG X AI & Software), global topic lead for transportation infrastructure and airport, and AP regional sector lead for travel and tourism. I also held positions as the SEA People Chair and Office Head for BCG Kuala Lumpur.

Prior to my time at BCG, I spent 16 years in the tech industry. I held leadership roles at Cisco Systems and HP, where I worked on mission-critical system development, product development, and technical marketing. In my first job, I researched and developed facial image recognition applications using neural network algorithms at the Singapore Agency for Science, Technology, and Research. During the early 90s, I founded Asia Cybermart, an e-commerce website specializing in sports merchandise.

I hold an MBA from the University of Chicago Graduate School of Business and a Bachelor of Science in Computer Science from the National University of Singapore.

slides.title:
Governance and Accountability: 
Achieving Infrastructure Goals with Coordinated Governance
slides.subtitle: Parth Doshi on LinkedIn
slides.description: By: Parth Doshi, Selin Zalma, Meldon Wolfgang, Stuart Westgate, Misha Osanov In the race to modernize and revitalize America’s aging infrastructure, one essential, yet overlooked, engine can accelerate progress: Governance. As the nation undertakes ambitious projects to upgrade roads, bridges, energy systems, and more, a solid foundation of effective decision-making, responsible resource allocation, and transparent oversight is critical to ensure the U.S. delivers on its goal of modernizing our national infrastructure efficiently and rapidly. Large capital projects commonly fail to deliver on-time or on-budget. For the $1T in funding from the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (IIJA), the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA), and Creating Helpful Incentives to Produce Semiconductors (CHIPS), that could mean billions in dollars wasted on inefficient governance from the states (e.g., cost overruns). During construction to treat radioactive material from the former Hanford nuclear weapons site in Washington – one of the U.S.’s most significant environmental infrastructure projects – DoE announced a 17-year delay and a cost overrun of $17B vs. the $4B estimated 20 years ago. Beyond inefficiency alone, fraud is another issue that can be mitigated with effective governance: while an estimated 5-7% is historically lost in government outlays to fraud, the Recovery Act had estimated fraud rates of only 1%, largely credited to its Recovery Board. For the sake of both efficiency and effectiveness, states must develop a thoughtful governance strategy to ensure good stewardship of funds and acceleration of delivery for priority infrastructure projects. This article discusses common challenges limiting the effectiveness of state infrastructure planning and presents a series of recommended actions that states can adopt to drive their infrastructure initiatives towards a more efficient, resilient, and robust future. Following up on our tenth article on Operations and Maintenance, we continue our series Bridging the Gap: Propelling America’s Public Infrastructure Forward with an in-depth look at the actions leaders can take to set the foundation for strong governance. The case for governance Governance refers to the processes, structures, and mechanisms through which authority is exercised and decisions are made in an organization. Governance spans the full lifecycle of an infrastructure project, including policy formulation, planning, implementation, and monitoring, all of which are crucial for successful infrastructure planning and development. Proper governance ensures infrastructure projects are aligned to a government’s goals and facilitates the engagement of stakeholders, leading to better-informed decisions and wider project acceptance. Once infrastructure projects are underway, governance mechanisms play a crucial role in monitoring progress, evaluating outcomes, and enabling necessary adjustments to ensure that projects stay on track and deliver expected benefits. During the Covid-19 emergency, many state governments effectively created governance structures to orchestrate complex webs of stakeholders, swiftly deploy resources, and continuously monitor progress. Now, state governments need to flex that muscle again in a more sustainable, longer-term fashion. Current state practices leave projects disjointed and ineffective Even with an unprecedented $1T in funding across IIJA, IRA, and CHIPS, state and local governments will find themselves behind schedule, over budget, and failing to meet infrastructure improvement goals if they don’t address the following common shortfalls in their governance and accountability practices: Absence of coordinating body to oversee infrastructure portfolio: Without formal stakeholder coordination, continuity in project delivery, and cross-disciplinary expertise, projects can run behind schedule and over budget. Current funding applications and approvals are siloed: Without a central location for all funding applications, states will struggle to allocate capital efficiently, prioritize across projects under different funding umbrellas, and prevent extra work for local planning bodies with limited resources. Infrastructure planning and budgeting is being done without thoughtful integration of input from regional and local levels: A disconnect between state planning and the impacted communities and regions leads to infrastructure that does not meet regional and local needs. On the other hand, simply serving as a middleman that conducts a pass-through of requests from the local level may result in a hodgepodge of projects that do not serve an integrated plan. Without proactive and thoughtful coordination and integration between states and their regional and local leadership, funds are misappropriated to ineffective or subscale projects. Private sector has limited involvement in infrastructure planning process: As mentioned in Article 2 second article of our Bridging the Gap series, with proper coordination every $1 of state funding can yield an additional $3.80 of private investment. This underscores the critical need for enhanced engagement and partnership between the public and private sectors in the infrastructure domain to ensure states use all available funds. In a striking example of the opportunity at hand, states can realize an estimated 18 - 33% CAPEX savings by integrating broadband and electricity distribution into other infrastructure projects like highway expansion, an endeavor that would not be possible without a well-organized, dedicated coordinating body. However, only a third of states have dedicated infrastructure agencies, while the remainder run their infrastructure strategy out of state agencies like the DOT or Office of Economic Development, leading to potential fragmentation or misalignment of priorities. While this example only highlights a potential financial outcome, state coordinating bodies would also serve to better accomplish non-financial objectives (e.g., safety, sustainability, etc.). Simplifying state governance through consolidation and delegation The following strategies can accelerate project delivery, prioritize regional needs, and bolster infrastructure resilience: Create a state infrastructure hub to accelerate project delivery and support best practices Consolidate grant funding applications into a universal application portal Define funding methodology to incorporate regional plans into state grant allocations Incorporate private sector stakeholders into initial infrastructure planning Create a dedicated infrastructure hub to accelerate project delivery and support best practices The creation of a state infrastructure hub can accelerate critical projects by providing rapid coordination, technical expertise, and regulatory support. This central body can aid in project planning, engage stakeholders, and mobilize resources, ensuring efficient implementation of infrastructure initiatives, and maintaining project management continuity. A program management office (PMO) within the hub drives the state's infrastructure development effort by offering targeted assistance in areas such as design optimization, risk management, and emergency response. Recommended actions for states: Establish clear policies and frameworks that outline the hub’s operational procedures, including guidelines for resource allocation, stakeholder communication, and knowledge transfer. Create mechanisms within the hub for regular communication and data sharing with other state agencies and local development councils Appoint a dedicated team of experts to function as a PMO within the hub that can oversee infrastructure planning and coordination. We dedicated two articles to the composition and implementation of infrastructure hubs to begin our Bridging the Gap series; for more information, you can access them here: Infrastructure Hub: Planning and Prioritizing Infrastructure Investments at the Portfolio Level A Hub of Opportunity: How State Agency Coordination and Accountability Can Unleash Federal Funding. Consolidate grant funding applications into universal application portal Separate and disjointed state-level grant applications impose an unnecessary burden on regional and local development councils that are already resource constrained. By consolidating grant applications into a single portal, states can develop a more complete understanding of funding needs, find overlap to assist in coordination between local bodies, and distribute funds more efficiently based on state priorities, all while relieving that undue burden on local entities. This consolidated location would serve as: Single portal for all applications Master page to avoid reentering basic information across separate applications Website that gives real time feedback on application completeness or errors FAQs that are shared with all bidders, and Master list of projects across infrastructure types by geography to support synergies Recommended actions for states: Develop and implement a new, centralized grant application portal through which regional and local development councils will submit all funding requests. Consolidate application review team to sort, evaluate, and prioritize applications based on state and local need, ensuring proper grant qualifications for each project. Develop protocol to help identify synergies between regional development councils with overlapping priorities and enable better coordination. Define funding methodology to incorporate regional plans into state grant allocations Empowering regional development councils to give critical input into decision-making surrounding state-level support can help expedite critical projects that may otherwise be halted by regulatory tie-ups or funding shortfalls. Recommended actions for states: Incorporate regional development councils in budget planning to ensure important input and perspectives are visible at state level. Establish regular meetings to discuss regional development priorities and earmark funds for priority projects. Proactively identify roadblocks that development councils may face to draft legislative or executive relief for local permitting override. Incorporate private sector stakeholders into initial infrastructure planning States hold the potential to amplify the effectiveness and sustainability of infrastructure projects by integrating private stakeholders into the preliminary phases of planning. Engaging private entities from the outset of infrastructure projects can harness their specialized expertise, financial resources, and innovative thinking to create a more robust and comprehensive infrastructure strategy. Recommended actions for states: Plan and execute Public-Private Collaborative Workshops where government officials, public agencies, and private stakeholders can convene to brainstorm, discuss ideas, and collaborate on infrastructure projects. Design incentive frameworks that encourage private sector participation in early-stage infrastructure planning, including tax incentives, grants, or preferential access to project contracts for private entities that contribute to project conceptualization and feasibility assessment. Institute NDAs and data sharing and protection agreements to foster trust among stakeholders for long-term, beneficial relationships. A Case Study New York State's Empire State Development (ESD) exemplifies how strategic governance can impact project planning and delivery. Launch of the Consolidated Funding Application (CFA) ESD created the CFA to streamline grant application process through a single, easy-to-use-portal. CFA allows users to apply for all applicable regional funding sources at once and reduces overhead necessary to write and review funding applications. Consolidated application allows regional economic development councils to allocate funding for regional priorities via CFA before going to relevant distributing agency Funding methodology that incorporates regional prioritization plans Regional economic development councils (REDCs) prioritize projects for allocation of ~$650M earmarked for regional economic & infrastructure development. ESD has given authority to accelerate project timelines for priority projects (including Hudson Yards subway extension and Moynihan Train Station) through state support, including: (a) Exemptions from local laws (e.g., zoning and regulations that can delay or risk project delivery) and (b) Authority to issue bonds without referendum, grant loans, and acquire property. An implementation plan that gets results ESD effectively manages a $3-4B budget that is allocated among regions based on prioritization. $7.5B has been distributed through regional economic development councils to 9,300 projects since 2011. ESD has successfully managed 8 signature projects, due to the freedom gained by delegating regional projects to REDCs. Priority subsidiaries support development of regions in tandem with state planning priorities (e.g., Harlem community development). Closing thoughts States have an extraordinary opportunity to transform their aging infrastructure, but diligent execution depends on their ability to drive governance and accountability. As shown in the New York ESD example and demonstrated by other jurisdictions like the United Kingdom’s Infrastructure and Projects Authority and Australia’s Infrastructure New South Wales, proper governance enables regional planning to drive state outcomes and increase the efficiency and effectiveness of infrastructure projects. State agencies and key stakeholders must act today by identifying shortfalls in their own infrastructure planning systems and determine how best to delegate and consolidate for efficient, coordinated planning. By leveraging learnings from recent federal funding projects, states can establish a robust governance strategy for the increasingly complex and large-scale infrastructure investments of the coming years. Be on the lookout for the next and final article in our series, Metrics Development and Tracking: Driving Transparency and Accountability to Achieve Success, which will cover how to leverage your data to improve transparency and enable better decision making. publications.title: Build or Buy: Strategically Sourcing Your Generative AI Foundation Model in a Rapidly Evolving Market
publications.description:
As companies begin developing GenAI solutions, they will have to choose whether to rely on third-party FMs or build their own — a choice that, due to the fundamental nature of these models, can dictate these companies’ entire GenAI strategy. 

While we don’t have a crystal ball, we attempt to answer 4 core questions to guide companies in their FM decision making process:
1) What are the economics of GenAI?
2) Where should you play across the GenAI landscape?
3) How is the FM market likely to evolve?
4) What are the critical considerations when sourcing a GenAI FM?

publications.title: Can A.I. Stop Fake News?
publications.description: The spread of disinformation illuminates algorithms’ unique abilities and shortcomings.

publications.title: Case Studies: Artificial Intelligence
publications.description: Case studies on Artificial Intelligence for large enterprises, VC firms, consulting firms, and product strategy / development teams.

publications.title: For A.I. Companies, Technology Is Inherent in Strategy
publications.description: There’s a tendency among many entrepreneurs and other executives to separate strategy from technological development. Many companies want to figure out every stage of their product’s evolution without thinking through what it will take to realize those steps. But if the centerpiece of your product is artificial intelligence, technology and strategy are inseparable.

publications.title: From Apps to Agents: How the AI-Native Tech Stack Is Transforming Software
publications.description:
The rise of AI agents is getting all the attention but quietly behind the scenes the underlying tech stack of apps is changing too. This article explores the seismic shifts in the emerging AI-native tech stack—resulting in more complex reasoning capabilities and execution of non-deterministic tasks autonomously. 
 
In this article we aim to answer 4 core questions: 

1. What does the new tech stack for AI-native apps look like and what new functionality does it enable?
2. How can this new tech stack support increased innovation in agentic AI apps?
3. Which parts of the stack are key differentiators and increase the right to win for AI-native apps?
4. What should app developers, app platforms, and data platforms do to support AI-native apps in the future?

publications.title: Leveraging Generative AI for the Software Industry
publications.description: Gen AI is the hot topic right now and will even disrupt software development. There are a few key questions we have to answer: How can software developers leverage generative AI? What opportunities are there for the tech industry?

publications.title: Orchestration: The New Mission Critical Capability in an Agentic Future
publications.description:
Billions of AI agents are on the horizon. But the real question is: who will orchestrate them?
 
Developers are calling orchestration the “secret sauce” of agentic AI — something that permeates the way individual agents are built, how prompts are broken down and sent to specific LLMs, how answers are refined before being sent back to the user, as well as how a network of agents works together. Different than Model Context Protocol (MCP), which acts as a communication standard, orchestration is the coordination layer that manages multiple agents collaborating on complex tasks. We believe that orchestration will act as the central nervous system for “agent-first” organizations, and that there is both an opportunity and imperative for existing software vendors to provide this capability.

publications.title: Rethinking B2B Software Pricing in the Agentic AI Era
publications.description: The rapid rise of AI agents is redefining how B2B software vendors capture value. In this new era, software vendors must not only determine which types of agentic AI capabilities to offer but also make two critical pricing-related decisions. First, they need to decide how to package AI agents and broader AI-powered innovations: incrementally, as additional features on top of existing solutions, or included in current offerings. Second, they must figure out how to transition from user-based subscriptions to pricing models better aligned with value delivered, while simultaneously mitigating the risk of revenue loss.

publications.title: Sustaining competitive advantage in software in the world of Generative AI
publications.description:
“Software is eating the world, but AI will eat software.” This has been a maxim in the tech sector for several years but has never felt truer than it does now with the rise of generative AI.

We don’t have a crystal ball, but we aim to answer two fundamental questions:
1. Will generative AI disrupt my enterprise software (SW) business?
2. What do I need to do to retain competitive advantage?

publications.title: Your Software Customers Need a Tailored Industry Approach
publications.description: A range of industry-specific challenges, from various regulatory requirements to fragmented technology stacks, have led today’s B2B software buyers to expect vendor solutions that are custom-fit for their distinct needs. In response, software companies are increasingly “verticalizing”—adapting their products, marketing, sales, and ecosystems to specific industry use cases—rather than relying on the broad applicability of “horizontal” products.

headline: Senior Partner and Managing Director  at Boston Consulting Group (BCG) - Insurance, Technology & Digital Advantage
about:
Nadine Moore is a recognized leader in the global insurance and financial services industry, with over 25 years of experience spanning insurance carriers, brokers, reinsurers, and private equity-backed firms. She is a trusted advisor to C-suite executives and investors, helping organizations unlock economic value, drive profitable growth, and navigate complex market dynamics. 
 
As Boston Consulting Group’s (BCG) Global Topic Leader for Property & Casualty, Commercial Insurance, and Reinsurance, Nadine works with insurers, reinsurers and brokers to deploy AI and digital transformation strategies that enhance growth strategies and core capabilities including underwriting, claims, and risk management.  Inside BCG Nadine is highly regarded as a people builder, helping grow her colleagues and creating pathways for their success.  Nadine is a well-known advisor to private investors in the insurance sector, with a particular depth in insurance brokerage and Insurtech.  Her expertise in cyber insurance, fraud prevention, and intangible risks positions her as a thought leader in the evolving landscape of cybersecurity and risk mitigation.
 
Prior to joining BCG, Nadine was a Managing Director and Practice Leader at Accenture, where she led large-scale transformations for insurance and financial services clients across the United States, Canada, and the United Kingdom.
 
Her ability to blend pragmatic industry knowledge with cutting-edge technology has made her a sought-after advisor for private equity firms, insurers, and financial institutions looking to optimize performance, execute M&A strategies, and drive operational excellence.  Her leadership style is genuine and engaging.
 
A licensed Property & Casualty, Life, and Health Insurance broker, Nadine is frequently featured in industry media for her expertise in cyber insurance, digital innovation, and regulatory trends. She is widely respected for her ability to solve complex challenges, foster high-performing teams, and deliver measurable impact.
 
In addition to her professional achievements, Nadine serves on the Board of the Northern Illinois Food Bank, where she is treasurer.  Nadine also contributes to food security efforts through strategic initiatives and partnerships across the BCG network.
 
Outside of work, she enjoys hands-on projects, fitness, and spending time with family.

publications.title: A New Architecture to Manage Data Costs and Complexity
publications.description:
Few infrastructure technology markets have moved as quickly as data management, analytics, and artificial intelligence (AI). With data volumes growing exponentially and the data stack continuing to undergo rapid innovation, companies are struggling to keep pace. It’s a dilemma that executives must overcome not only because data and analytics are strategic imperatives but also because the associated costs are enormous and unsustainable. This combination of complexity and costs is hurtling many companies toward a cliff that could cripple operations.

To avoid falling off this precipice, companies must adopt a fundamentally different approach to their architectures: a more federated and distributed paradigm. BCG research has determined that, in many cases, this approach will allow companies to solve the challenges of data access and integration in a siloed data landscape and accelerate innovation while maintaining the ability to leverage legacy data stores.

publications.title: Adopting an Ecosystem-First Mindset in Software
publications.description:
As technology becomes ever more crucial for business, companies face many challenges in realizing its benefits. Buying centers proliferate across their enterprise, data security and privacy face increasingly sophisticated threats, and modernizing legacy systems and moving to cloud is a protracted process that becomes more complex each year. By building a robust ecosystem of partners, software firms can better help their customers navigate these challenges—and enjoy a clear competitive advantage.

This is possible because of the diverse capabilities of robust, modern ecosystems that have emerged with the shift to cloud and subscription models. No longer are software firms’ partners merely “channels” for transacting and fulfilling sales in traditional sell-and-service business models. Instead, they can now play an end-to-end role across the entire lifecycle, helping customers accelerate their digital transformation.

publications.title: When Time Isn't Money: An Analysis of Early Voting and Campaign Spending
publications.publishedAt: The Columbia Journal of Politics and Society · Apr 1, 2011
publications.description: Despite the increasing significance of early voting in United States elections, much of the academic research on campaigns specifically on campaign expenditures—fails to account for the role of early voters. This study uses newly available data from the Federal Election Commission and Congressional Quarterly and two regression models to establish the impact of early voting on expenditure timing and the impact of early spending on candidate vote share. It finds that while campaigns in states with early voting spend their funds significantly earlier than campaigns in states without early voting, this spending does not bring with it an apparent electoral advantage. This validates claims made by campaign experts and news media about earlier spending, guides the expenditures of campaigns, and challenges the academic literature to account for early voting.

publications.title: Bias in the Perceived Prevalence of Open Defecation
publications.description: People often form perceptions about how prevalent a behavior is in a social group. However, these perceptions can be inaccurate and biased. While persistent undesirable practices in low-income countries have drawn global attention, evidence regarding people’s perception of how prevalent these practices are is scarce. Among those harmful practices, open defecation in India remains a significant public health concern, where it perpetuates the vicious cycle of disease and poverty. In this study, we focus on measuring the perceived prevalence of open defecation among respondents in Bihar, India. We examined the bias in perceived prevalence, which is defined as a pattern of deviation from the actual prevalence of open defecation. Results showed that respondents who defecate in the open overestimate the prevalence of open defecation, whereas those who consistently use toilets underestimate it. This finding suggests a false consensus bias in the perceived prevalence of open defecation. Scholars, policymakers, and program implementers who seek to correct misperceptions about open defecation by broadcasting real prevalence should be aware of biases in the perceived prevalence and address them in behavior change interventions.

publications.title: Which grades are better, A’s and C’s or all B’s? Effects of variability in grades on mock college admissions decisions
publications.description: Students may need to decide whether to invest limited resources evenly across all courses and thus end with moderate grades in all, or focus on some of the courses and thus end with variable grades. This study examined which pattern of grades is perceived more favorably. When judging competency, people give more weight to positive than negative information, in which case heterogeneous grades would be perceived more favorably as they have more positive grades than homogeneous moderate grades. Furthermore, high school students are told to demonstrate their passion in college applications. Nonetheless, people generally overweigh negative information, which can result in a preference for a student with homogeneous grades lacking extremely negative grades. The college admissions decisions in particular may also involve emphasis on long-term stable, consistent, and responsible character, which the homogeneous grades may imply. Study 1 found that laypeople, undergraduate students, and admissions officers preferred to admit a student with homogeneous grades to a college than a student with heterogeneous grades even when their GPAs were the same. Study 2 used a heterogeneous transcript signaling a stereotypic STEM or humanities student, and found that while undergraduate students were more split in their choices, laypeople and admissions officers still preferred a student with homogeneous grades. Study 3 further replicated the preference for a student with homogeneous grades by using higher or lower average GPAs and wider or narrower range of grades for the heterogeneous grades. Possible reasons and limitations of the studies are discussed.

publications.title: How trendsetters shaped India’s massive sanitation campaign
publications.description: The Swachh Bharat Mission (SBM) is the Indian government’s largest sanitation program to date with a projected cost of $28 billion. By most accounts Swachh Bharat has had a major impact on sanitation in India. Beyond its impact, the program is noteworthy for its size and the speed at which it grew. A team of researchers at Penn’s Center for Social Norms and Behavioral Dynamics investigated the role of trendsetters and change agents in the campaign’s growth. With the use of qualitative interviews, they point to several personal, social and organizational factors that have supported its growth

publications.title: When is science considered interesting and important?
publications.description: Scientists seek to discover truths that are interesting and important. We characterized these notions by asking laypeople to assess the importance, interestingness, surprisingness, practical value, scientific impact, and comprehensibility of research reported in the journals Science and Psychological Science. These judgments were interrelated in both samples, with interest predicted by practical value, surprisingness, and comprehensibility, and importance predicted mainly by practical value. However, these judgments poorly tracked the academic impact of the research, measured by citation counts three and seven years later. These results suggest that although people have internally reliable notions of what makes science interesting and important, these notions do not track scientific findings’ actual impact

publications.title: Shrieking Sirens. Schemata, scripts, and social norms: How change occurs
publications.description: This essay investigates the relationships among scripts, schemata, and social norms. The authors examine how social norms are triggered by particular schemata and are grounded in scripts. Just as schemata are embedded in a network, so too are social norms, and they can be primed through spreading activation. Moreover, the expectations that allow a social norm’s existence are inherently grounded in particular scripts and schemata. Using interventions that have targeted gender norms, open defecation, female genital cutting, and other collective issues as examples, the authors argue that ignoring the cognitive underpinnings of a social norm can hamper the effectiveness of behavioral interventions.

publications.title: Phase 1 Project Report. Social Networks and Norms: Sanitation in Bihar and Tamil Nadu, India
publications.description:
This report summarizes the findings of the first wave of the Penn Social Norms Group (Penn SoNG) open defecation research project, conducted in rural and urban Bihar and Tamil Nadu, India. This research is part of a larger, three-year project designed to identify the social factors that affect individuals’ propensity to engage in open defecation above and beyond infrastructure limitations. In this report, we
discuss baseline usage and ownership rates, and how these rates diverge from previous research data. We then provide an analysis of the novel social network approach used in this study as applied to open defecation, investigating which networks are the most important to individuals when deciding to own
and/or use a latrine as well as demographic patterns within these networks.

publications.title: Phase 2 Project Report. Social Networks and Norms: Sanitation in Bihar and Tamil Nadu, India
publications.description:
This report summarizes the findings on the second wave of the Penn Social Norms Group (Penn SoNG) open defecation research project, conducted in rural and urban Bihar and Tamil Nadu, India. This research is part of a larger, three-year project designed to identify the social factors that affect one’s propensity to engage in open defecation above and beyond infrastructure limitations. In this report, we
discuss baseline usage and ownership rates, and how these rates diverge from previous research. We then provide an analysis of the novel social network approach used in this study as applied to open defecation, investigating what types of network members are the most important to individuals when
deciding to own and/or use a latrine as well as demographic patterns within these networks.

publications.title: Beyond the Product: Service Expansion Opportunities for MedTechs
publications.description:
Historically, an evolution toward high-value services has been a natural part of the development of hardware tech companies. Hospital systems in the U.S. and other developed markets are looking to centralize and coordinate supply chains more effectively. This increasing demand from customers—as well as competitive pressure from low-cost Asian device companies—will force established MedTechs to introduce ancillary service offerings around their core hardware products.

Several MedTechs are already developing broader solutions, but the shift doesn’t come naturally to many companies that traditionally put “product excellence” above “customer excellence.”  

This Executive Insights discusses the need for innovation in a shifting healthcare landscape. Like hospital systems, consolidation among MedTechs will almost certainly happen, and survivorship in this area will be determined by innovative services and solutions.

publications.title: Does Your Corporate IQ Measure Up to Your Medical Technology Peers?
publications.description: This article focuses on your Medical Technology Corporate IQsm, which measures a corporation's success at innovation relative to its peer group. Measuring and monitoring your company's innovation rate and Corporate IQ can help management teams make the tough choices, and even when faced with the pressures of day-to-day performance create value for the long term.

publications.title: Guest Blog: L.E.K. Forecasts GPO Growth, Spotlights Purchasing Trends by Hospital Size
publications.description: Unprecedented cost pressures on hospitals will play a pivotal role in driving GPO growth, according to L.E.K. Consulting’s Strategic Hospital Priorities Study. L.E.K.’s third annual study of nearly 200 senior hospital decision-makers tracks changes in hospital strategies and purchasing trends. More than 60% of U.S. hospital executives surveyed expect budget increases in 2012, a trend that is expected to continue during the next five years. But despite growing budgets, 80% of administrators asked are continuing their aggressive supplier negotiations in an effort to manage costs – and the use of GPOs will continue to play a central role in their procurement strategies.

publications.title: Healthcare Reform Shifts Hospital Priorities, Creates New Opportunities for MedTech Companies
publications.description:
L.E.K.’s new study reveals how hospital executives are shifting their purchasing priorities amid looming healthcare reform mandates and existing economic constraints. The second annual L.E.K. Strategic Hospital Priorities Study also ranks hospital purchasing criteria for MedTech products and identifies new opportunities for MedTech vendors.

The study provides important new survey findings from senior hospital executives that include:

- Hospital budget forecasts for the next five years 
- Key areas where hospitals plan to increase spending 
- New strategies for complying with healthcare insurance mandates 
- How MedTech purchasing criteria is changing 
- Areas where MedTech providers can capitalize on new hospital needs

publications.title: Hospitals Adopt New Strategies to Boost Profitability, but Still Face Deep Challenges: A New Imperative for MedTech
publications.description:
Demand for healthcare services continues to rise due to an aging population, rising obesity, higher rates of chronic disease, and expansion of healthcare coverage. Yet for most hospitals, top-line growth is not keeping pace with strong industry headwinds. In the coming years already-low margins will be further squeezed by rising enrollments in Medicare and Medicaid, as well as significant investments in IT and facilities.

To remain viable hospitals are exploring new sources of added value, from integration of care and partnerships with payers, to outsourcing and competitive differentiation. MedTech companies will need to evolve too, working harder to understand their customers’ complex business challenges and adopting new models to serve them. The fourth annual L.E.K. Hospital Priorities Study explores major industry trends, and how MedTech companies can partner with hospitals to overcome the significant hurdles they face.

publications.title: Hospitals Apply Surgical Precision to Budgets, Brace to Support Healthcare Reform
publications.description:
The L.E.K. Consulting Strategic Hospital Priorities Study provides insight into budgeting trends that span all hospital operations and impact specific departments. The evolution of hospital purchasing decisions reveals important opportunities and ramifications for the companies that serve the hospital community – medical device and life sciences companies, hospital equipment manufacturers, healthcare service providers, and information technology (IT) vendors.

L.E.K.’s study offers unique insight from more than 200 senior hospital decision makers in the areas of general hospital trends, hospital strategy, unmet needs and legislative reform. In addition, the first annual study provides department-specific purchasing insight into more than a dozen clinical and administrative areas.

publications.title: Hospitals Rethink MedTech Purchasing Strategies as Budgets Grow
publications.description:
Many hospitals have weathered the economic downturn that forced dramatic spending cuts and are now refocusing on strategic initiatives. L.E.K.’s research also shows that although many hospital budgets are growing, health executives are still scrutinizing purchases and are using multiple channels to procure MedTech products at highly competitive prices.

Insights from our third annual L.E.K. Strategic Hospital Priorities Study include:

- Hospital budget forecasts for the next five years 
- Key areas where hospitals plan to increase spending 
- Healthcare reform’s impact on purchasing decisions 
- The growing role that government purchasing organizations (GPOs) are playing in hospital procurement 
- How MedTech companies need to respond to changing hospital purchasing priorities 
- Areas where MedTech providers can capitalize on new hospital needs

publications.title: Mergers & Acquisitions: Preparing Your Company to Win
publications.description: Buying your way to success through acquisitions is an alluring prospect in today’s slow-moving economic environment, but a tricky one to get right. L.E.K. Consulting analyzed more than 2,500 M&A deals between 1993 and 2010 and uncovered an interesting trend: M&A performance is generally better among frequent acquirers. Experience and repetition matter. So what are the skills that frequent acquirers develop that gives them an M&A advantage, and how can any company—regardless of M&A experience--obtain them? This Executive Insights answers the key questions that any executive should consider before embarking on an M&A strategy. L.E.K.’s Michael Connerty and Bob Lavoie explore the five steps that any company can undertake to prepare their organizations to create shareholder value through acquisitions.

publications.title: Mergers & Acquisitions: What Winnders Do to Beat the Odds
publications.description: Activity in M&A often comes in bursts. As of the second quarter of 2013, the scent is in the air. Company management is flush with cash, bolstered by buoyant share prices, and face slow prospects for organic growth. But capturing value by creating a whole that is greater than the sum of its parts is risky. Recently, L.E.K. Consulting analyzed the performance of more than 2,500 M&As between 1993 and 2010 – a period that included two boom and bust economic cycles. L.E.K. found that nearly 60% of companies destroyed shareholder value after the deal closed. In this new Executive Insights, L.E.K. shares how management can overcome common pitfalls to beat the long odds of creating value through mergers and acquisitions. From identifying the right target to synergy valuation to post-merger integration, winners have shown that with the right approach, value through M&A can be found and captured.
